items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Proposals Submission Deadline: July 17, 2026 Full Chapters Due: October 30, 2026 Submission Date: October 30, 2026 Introduction This edited collection features scholarly voices with attention to horror in its transmedia representations, including film, literature, comics, art, branding, and more. Chapters give attention to the ways that fans take up the realities and ideas presented in horror, the affordances of the genre, and participation in this network of storytelling. The reactions of readers/viewers/fans, the decisions of creatives, the presentation of ideas within particular forms of media, and more form elements of the researched conversation in this volume. Objective This collection seeks to advance conversation about the theoretical functions of horror across media including notions of adaptation and literary/literacy-based choices in the work. This includes, but is not limited to, design structures, cultural influences, the role of lore, (re)considerations of the monstrous, embodiment in the genre, sub-genre considerations, and more. Target Audience This book is intended for academics in media, literacy, literature, communication, and interdisciplinary fields. Students enrolled in courses in these fields can benefit from this knowledge as they pursue courses of study and further academic work in these disciplines. Recommended Topics Emotional and Philosophical Reactions to Horror Media Themes and Interactions across Media Representations in the Genre Adaptation Processes/Decisions/Designs in Horror across Media Studies of Narrative and Response/Interpretation Recent Trends/Movements in Horror Theoretical Approaches to Horror Composition/Representation Analysis of Race, Gender, Class in Horror Considerations and Reconsiderations of the Monstrous Author/Creator Decisions and Purposes in the Genre/across Media Horror Character and Author/Director Studies Critical and Analytical Work on Embodiment in Horror Critical and Analytical Examinations of Cultural Stories in the Genre The Role of Lore/Mythology in Horror Studies of Writing/Creating Processes in the Genre Fandom Communities, Fan Fiction, Cosplay, and Other Responses Submission Procedure Researchers and practitioners are invited to submit on or before July 17, 2026, a chapter proposal of 1,000 to 2,000 words clearly explaining the mission and concerns of his or her proposed chapter. Authors will be notified by July 31, 2026 about the status of their proposals and sent chapter guidelines.Full chapters of a minimum of 10,000 words (word count includes references and related readings) are expected to be submitted by October 30, 2026, and all interested authors must consult the guidelines for manuscript submissions at https://www.igi-global.com/publish/contributor-resources/before-you-write/ prior to submission. All submitted chapters will be reviewed on a double-anonymized review basis. Contributors may also be requested to serve as reviewers for this project. Note: There are no submission or acceptance fees for manuscripts submitted to this book publication, Theory and Practice in Horror Transmedia Fandom and Creation. All manuscripts are accepted based on a double-anonymized peer review editorial process. All proposals should be submitted through the eEditorial Discovery® online submission manager. Publisher This book is scheduled to be published by IGI Global Scientific Publishing, an international academic publisher of the "Information Science Reference", "Medical Information Science Reference", "Business Science Reference", and "Engineering Science Reference" imprints. IGI Global Scientific Publishing specializes in publishing reference books, scholarly journals, and electronic databases featuring academic research on a variety of innovative topic areas including, but not limited to, education, social science, medicine and healthcare, business and management, information science and technology, engineering, public administration, library and information science, media and communication studies, and environmental science. For additional information regarding the publisher, please visit https://www.igi-global.com. This publication is anticipated to be released in 2027. Indexing Information for Prospective Authors IGI Global Scientific Publishing meets the criteria for inclusion in major indexing services such as Scopus; however, it is important to note that all indexing decisions are made independently by these services. IGI Global Scientific Publishing books are selectively indexed by the indexing organization after publication. Indexing cannot be guaranteed for any book prior to publication, and the indexing organization has complete control over the final selection and timeline. Important Dates July 17, 2026: Proposal Submission Deadline July 31, 2026: Notification of Acceptance October 30, 2026: Full Chapter Submission January 1, 2027: Review Results Returned February 12, 2027: Final Acceptance Notification February 26, 2027: Final Chapter Submission Inquiries Jason DeHart University of Tennessee Knoxville dehartjason33@gmail.com Classifications Education; Library and Information Science; Media and Communications; Social Sciences and Humanities

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR CHAPTERS The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature Editors: Mariusz Finkielsztein (University of Gdan?sk) mariusz.finkielsztein@gmail.com Josefa Ros Velasco (Complutense University of Madrid) josros@ucm.es The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature is to be a comprehensive monographic study examining boredom as a central aesthetic, philosophical, psychological, and socio-cultural category in the history of modern literature. Rather than relying purely on abstract theory, this volume approaches boredom through focused case studies devoted to individual authors and their works. Across these chapters, boredom-alongside adjacent states such as ennui, tedium, spleen, acedia, melancholy, existential malaise, and affective exhaustion-emerges variously as paralysis, protest, privilege, illness, and spiritual crisis. By situating close textual readings within the broader intellectual history of modernity, the volume, written by a multidisciplinary group of authors, is to demonstrate that literary boredom is a powerful diagnostic lens on social order, temporality, and the modern subject's experience of meaninglessness. Volume Structure & Epochal Scope The volume is planned as a Handbook or Companion and covers not only the most vital writers addressing the theme of boredom but also a broad selection of modern authors (around 60 chapters). The book is to trace the evolution of literary boredom across (tentatively) seven historical and thematic phases: Early Modernity & Enlightenment Foundations: Early reflections on existential void and social routine (e.g. Diderot, Laclos, Austen). Romantic Ennui (1770s-1840s): Melancholy, idealist frustration, and the world-weary anti-hero (e.g., Goethe, de Stae?l, Senancour, Byron, Chateaubriand, Constant, Stendhal, Sand, Balzac, Musset). The Superfluous Man: The Russian literary archetype of social paralysis, alienation, and unfulfilled potential (e.g. Pushkin, Lermontov, Goncharov, Turgenev). Bourgeois Boredom, Realism, & Decadent Spleen: Domestic stagnation, industrial monotony, social entrapment, and aesthetic decay (e.g., Dickens, Flaubert, Tolstoy, Fontane, Chopin, Ibsen, Gilman, Conrad, Chekhov, Baudelaire, Huysmans, Wilde). Modernist Stagnation (Early 20th C.): Temporal distortion, consciousness, alienation, and metaphysical paralysis (e.g., Proust, Joyce, Pessoa, Mann, Kafka, Woolf). Catastrophism & Existential Absurdity (Mid-20th C.): Totalitarian dread, the absurdity of existence, and postwar existential malaise (e.g., Broch, Platonov, Orwell, H. Miller, Gombrowicz, Sartre, Camus, Beckett, Buzzati, Gracq). Postwar Emptiness, Consumerism, & Digital Fatigue: Mass society, late-capitalist hyper-consumption, information overload, and contemporary affective exhaustion (e.g., Moravia, Perec, de Beauvoir, Ernaux, Bellow, Bernhard, Duras, DeLillo, Houellebecq, Ferrante, Rourke, Moshfegh). Chapter Guidelines & Scope Each chapter must offer an in-depth analysis of the theme of broadly understood boredom in the work of a single author (according to a formula: Boredom in...). The title should include the name and surname of a writer as a main part, and a freely formulated subtitle. Analytical Approach: Authors may focus on a single representative work but should analyse boredom across multiple texts of an author to demonstrate how boredom functions as a recurring motif in the author's oeuvre. Target Audience: Written primarily for readers seeking to deepen their understanding of boredom in a specific author's work (spoilers are permitted), while remaining accessible to a general literary audience. Comparative analysis with other writers should be kept to a minimum. Required Contextual Elements: o Biographical Context: Key details situating the writer within their epoch. Where applicable, personal engagement with boredom (e.g., excerpts from letters, diaries) may be included. o Socio-Cultural Context: Historical background necessary to understand the specific societal structures depicting boredom (e.g., aristocratic class dynamics, marital systems, late-capitalist work environments, author's country history and socio-cultural context). Submission guidelines: The abstract of the proposed chapter (between 250-500 words) along with a short bio (up to 150 words) and contact information should be sent to editors via e-mail before the end of October 2026. Contributors may propose up to two chapters. Each submission must include a brief statement detailing: (a) how the chosen author's work relates to boredom; and (b) what the contributor's expertise is on the writer. The minimum criteria for inclusion of a writer are: the author must address themes of boredom/ennui, possess at least some international recognition, and be available in English translation. Poetry is excluded. The comments and decisions on the proposed chapters will be provided before the end of December 2026. Then, the proposal for the book will be sent to prospective publishers (Routledge Handbook Series, The Oxford Handbooks, The Cambridge Companions or The Palgrave Handbooks). In case of a positive answer from a publisher, the authors will be asked to prepare the chapter, between 6,000 and 8,000 words including footnotes and references. Technical information will be provided after the publisher accepts the proposal and will depend on the publisher's style. In case of any doubts and/or questions, we encourage prospective authors to consult the editors directly. Prospective deadline for chapters: mid-2028

items.fullDescription: John Steinbeck once remarked that fellow-Californian Robinson Jeffers wrote some the "greatest poetry since Whitman." Steinbeck kept a significant collection of Jeffers work both in his personal library and Ed Ricketts' Lab, where Jeffers was an influential topic in their endlessly varied conversations. When asked about possibility of meeting the poet, Steinbeck declined with a telling degree of reverence: "His poetry is perfect to me, and I don't think one should get the man mixed up with his work." Although they did eventually meet-notably when Steinbeck lived in Monterey in 1944-their relationship was one of distant, though friendly, mutual respect. Although these two writers rarely crossed physical paths, their work maintains a wide concurrence of concern. They both deeply engaged with Californian geography and history; they both emphasized the influence of the natural world upon the individual and society; they both had social circles that revolved around the Monterey Peninsula; they both were interested in psychoanalytical theory; they both were students of classical literature and philosophy; they both experienced extraordinary recognition at the peak of their literary fame (at one point, Jeffers was on the cover of Time magazine); they both were deeply uncomfortable with such a cultural spotlight; they both admonished personal humility in the face of environmental forces. Intersections such as these (and many more) deserve to be explored with more depth and significance. The editorial staff at the Steinbeck Review invites submissions for a special edition, "John Steinbeck and Robinson Jeffers." We are particularly interested in perspectives which put these authors into conversation in productive and even unexpected ways. Although submissions are not required to examine both authors, we strongly suggest that they engage (even if briefly) both Steinbeck and Jeffers. We welcome all critical and theoretical perspectives. Please see the full guide for submissions here and submit your paper to the Steinbeck Review's online submission system, found at www.editorialmanager.com/Steinbeck, no later than October 31, 2026. Decisions will be made by December 1, 2026. Submissions should be accompanied by an abstract and key words.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers - Siren! Magazine Second Issue: Disciplined Bodies, Transgressive Bodies, Transformed Bodies Link to the call: https://penn.manifoldapp.org/page/siren-current-call-for-proposals Bodies are shaped by the worlds we inhabit, the stories we tell about them, and the institutions through which we learn what a body is, what it should look like, how it should behave, and what it is permitted to become. Yet bodies are often treated as merely biological facts: fixed, self-evident, and prior to politics. This distinction matters because once something is understood as natural, the expectations attached to it can begin to appear inevitable. For this issue, we invite work on disciplined, transgressive, and transformed bodies. We are interested in work that reflects on how bodily norms are produced and enforced, what happens when bodies exceed or destabilize those norms, and how bodies are remade through political, social, technological, medical, aesthetic, and cultural processes. The question, then, is not only who tells bodies what to do, but how we come to understand what bodies are for in the first place and how we may challenge the constraints imposed over them. How do medicine, law, media, family, religion, workplaces, markets, states, and digital platforms make particular kinds of bodies appear normal, desirable, healthy, productive, legible, or valuable? What happens when a body does not fit the meaning assigned to it; when it refuses, cannot comply, fails to conform, or becomes something else? We are especially interested in moments when bodily categories begin to break down, when the meanings attached to bodies no longer hold, or become further reinforced and are resisted, and when bodies become sites of contradiction, refusal, negotiation, and possibility. Key terms For the purposes of this issue, we understand the three terms broadly and provisionally: Disciplined bodies are shaped by the norms, institutions, and expectations that surround them. They may be expected to reproduce, perform gender recognizably, be deemed healthy and desirable, remain productive and self-optimizing, regulate themselves, and stay intelligible to others. We welcome work on how these norms are produced, enforced, negotiated, and unevenly distributed. Transgressive bodies make those expectations difficult to sustain. Transgression need not be intentional: a body may refuse, fail, exceed, disrupt, or simply be unable to comply. Nor are particular bodies inherently transgressive; they are often rendered so by institutions and cultural frameworks that mark some forms of embodiment as abnormal, excessive, threatening, or unintelligible. Transformed bodies ask what happens when embodiments become a site of remaking. Bodies may be altered through medicine, technology, disability, transition, reproduction, labor, aging, artistic practice, environmental exposure, or political violence. Transformation may be desired or imposed, liberatory, or coercive. We are interested in what bodies become, what histories they carry, what forms of power shape them, and what futures they make imaginable. We welcome submissions that interpret one of these categories, bring two or more into conversation, question the distinctions between them, or propose other ways of thinking about bodily discipline, transgression, and transformation. Proposals should identify the term that most strongly connects to the submission while noting any significant intersections with the others. Possible topics may include, but are not limited to: -Bodily autonomy and reproductive rights -Disability and debility -Gender and sexuality -Race and racialization -Beauty and aesthetic labor -Health, illness, and wellness -Medicine and biomedical technologies -Aging -Death -War and militarization -Sport and physical performance -Embodiment and mediation (digital or otherwise) -Surveillance -Cyborg subjectivities -Body modification -Bodily aesthetics -Migration and borders -Carcerality -Labor and productivity -Environmental harm -Colonialism and its afterlives -Speculative or imagined forms of embodiment Who can submit We welcome work from scholars, students, artists, activists, independent researchers, and public intellectuals working in communication, media studies, feminist studies, cultural studies, disability studies, queer and trans studies, critical race studies, the humanities, and related fields. Submissions are open to contributors at all career stages, but we particularly encourage work from early-career scholars and those whose work may sit outside conventional academic publishing structures. Formats Submissions may be written, visual, audiovisual, audio, or hybrid. We welcome experimental forms alongside conventional scholarly approaches. Across formats, submissions should engage the issue's broader commitments to critical feminist inquiry, transnational solidarity, feminist world-making, and transformative social change. Timeline For full consideration, abstracts are due by October 31, 2026, with decisions made by December 10th. Completed submissions will be due by February 10th, 2027, with a projected publication date in September 2027. Guidelines for proposal types -Paper: Please send the title and a 250-word abstract outlining the argument for a full paper featuring an original contribution. Full papers are long-form (3000-5000 words) analytical essays that connect to the current topic of the issue. Please use the APA citation system for references. -Escalator Paper: Please submit the title and a 150-word abstract for a short analytical piece (500-2000 words). Research escalator papers are works-in-progress on novel ideas related to the issue theme; they will be published as submitted and paired with an expert mentor to develop into a full analytical or empirical work. Please use the APA citation system for references. -Multimedia and Hybrid Submissions: Please submit the title and a 200-250-word description explaining how your piece relates to the current issue's theme. For multimedia works, explain how text and other elements interact. Finished pieces should include a link to a sample. For works in progress, add a brief (up to 100 words) outline of the concept, your process, and the timeline for completion. Experimental submissions are encouraged. Important dates Abstract due: October 31, 2026 Acceptances: December 10, 2026 Final submission: February 10, 2027 Peer-review process and mentorships: February - June 2027 Expected publication date: early September 2027 All proposals should be sent as a .docx or .pdf document, and include a brief bio (up to 150 words) introducing yourself and your background. Please submit proposals to asc-sirenmagazine@asc.upenn.edu, using the subject line "Siren Magazine - Bodies." Direct any questions regarding the call or submission process to the same address.

items.fullDescription: Call for papers | Diffractions Issue 13 | The Aesthetics of Mythmaking: Narrative, Culture, and Power? Deadline for Abstracts: October 31st 2026 Deadline for Papers: January 31st 2027 Editors-in-Chief: Alyse Kaweng Fan, Thales Reis Alecrim? Call for papers | The Aesthetics of Mythmaking: Narrative, Culture, and Power "We are mythmaking creatures" (Ware 2025); human beings make and reinterpret myths. Mythmaking has remained a living action of the human cultural process since the earliest stage of human history. Myths are not static stories that stay unchanged across time; that is why agency and acts of mythmaking are powerful. Through mythmaking, inherited stories are continually adapted and reinterpreted to reflect changing cultural values and historical circumstances. Consequently, myth also assumes the form of a spectacle and ideology that must be critically examined; it often serves to naturalise or essentialise instances of domination, transforming contingent political agendas into "universal" truths. This call for papers values both the aesthetic brilliance of mythmaking in the arts and popular culture and the rigor critique of its ideological utility as a tool for hegemony. The inherent ambiguity of myth as both a meaning-making tool and a mechanism of control invites further scholarly exploration. We therefore seek to gather diverse perspectives on how these creative processes function across human experience, inviting interdisciplinary submissions that weave together multifaceted theories of myth and mythmaking.?? Even the same myth can be retold in radically different ways. For Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, the reinvented myth of Ozymandias represents a meditation on antiquity and the transience of glory. More than a century later, when Alan Moore rewrote Ozymandias in Watchmen, Shelley's ruined king was transformed into a morally ambiguous antagonist with the ambition to construct a new global saviour myth capable of uniting humanity. Moore's self-fashioned Ozymandias also evokes the myth of Superman, a figure that can be traced to Friedrich Nietzsche's concept (1883) of Übermensch (beyond-human). From Nietzschean philosophical ideal of self-overcoming, the Superman later takes forms in different myths: George Bernard Shaw's play and most famously in Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster's comics, where Superman represents the experiences and aspirations of Jewish immigrant communities before being incorporated into American national mythology during WWII and the Cold War. Superman mythmaking also transcended across the Pacific. In postwar Japan, superhumans like Astro-Boy and Ultraman reconstructed the archetype into social recovery and national renewal in the aftermath of atomic destruction. These examples show that mythmaking reinvents cultural symbols into new stories in response to political realities and collective memory. While myths are traditionally framed as archaic narratives of gods and heroes, modern scholars argue that the act of mythmaking can act as a mobilizing force in society and serves as a political power beyond its presence in art (Citton 2025; Josephson-Storm 2017). A political myth operates as a system of explanation, providing a cryptography through which the disconcerting chaos of contemporary facts is ordered and understood (Girardet 1987; Segal 2020). By offering an imaginary reading of a historical moment, myths restore intelligibility to a fractured world, manifesting in recurring structures like the nostalgia for a Golden Age or the yearning for a providential Saviour. However, this phenomenological reality of worldbuilding parallels Walter D. Mignolo's decolonial critique of "enunciation," where the content of myth is disseminated by the enunciator who ultimately possesses power (2018, 144-145).?? Mythmaking is still an ongoing cultural process without a singular definition. In a way, its study can be viewed as a consequence of the emergence of anthropology, which, during the 19th century, inquired about the concept of myth. This was the work of, for example, E.B. Tylor and J.G. Frazer. Yet, they were not so concerned about the aesthetics of mythmaking, as they viewed it as a form of "primitive knowledge" that was the exact opposite of Western art and science. Across the 20th century, authors as diverse as Bronislaw Malinowski (1922), Ernst Cassirer (1946), Claude Lévi-Strauss (1978), Northrop Frye (1967), Carl Jung (1964), Joseph Campbell (2004), and Mircea Eliade (1954) have suggested a whole range of different and often conflictive definitions for this concept. They actively engaged with the knowledge traditions of anthropology, philosophy, history, comparative literature, and religion studies.? One compelling form of analyzing mythmaking emerged at the intersection of aesthetics, philosophy, politics, and critical theory during the 19th century. Reacting against Enlightenment rationalism, German Romantics and Idealists such as Schiller, Schelling, and Hegel called for a "new mythology" to heal the alienation between humanity and nature while birthing the philosophical myth of absence-the belief that modernity is uniquely "mythless" (Josephson-Storm 2017, 17-21). This tension is central to the work of Max Horkheimer and Theodor Adorno, who, echoing Max Weber, argued that the Enlightenment's "disenchantment of the world" sought to dispel myths through reason, yet ultimately revealed that "enlightenment reverts to mythology" (2016, xviii), as instrumental rationality facilitated the domination of human beings over one another. In this way, inquiring the aesthetics of mythmaking involves a critique of different areas of the socio-cultural construct, reaching the realms of narrative, culture, and power.?? Amidst these diverse intellectual traditions and definitions of mythmaking, this call invites contributions that explore mythmaking as an ongoing process of cultural translation, forms of exercising power, political representation, and artistic (re)creation. We are interested in examining how mythmaking is still continually making, remaking, and mobilising new meanings and identities across historical periods, cultural contexts, and media forms. Proposals for thematic articles in response to this call are welcome, including but not limited to the following topics: ? Mythmaking and memory retelling? ? Superstition, hagiographies, and religion stories?? ? Mythmaking in different culturalforms: films, comics, and music? ? Mythmaking and Nationmaking?? ? Mythmaking as Tools of (De)colonial Discourse?? ? Mythmaking and Identity: theInvention of Tradition and Self-making? ? Mythmaking and Imaginary?? ? Lived experience and Phenomenology of Mythmaking ? The Power of Mythmaking in Social and Political Contexts? ? Mysticism and Poetry? ? Myth and Mythmaking in Literature from Romanticism to Modernism? ? Mythopoesia? ? Women Writers/Poets and Feminist Revisionist Mythmaking? ? The Role of Mythmaking in Visual Arts? ? The Study of Mythography in Modern Culture? ? Mythic ecology? ? Mythmaking, Philosophy, and Science: from myth to reason? ? Mythmaking and Psychology (Jungian Psychology, Psychoanalysis, etc)? Submissions and review process Abstracts will be received and reviewed by the Diffractions editorial board who will decide on the pertinence of proposals for the upcoming issue. After submission, we will get in touch with the authors of accepted abstracts in order to invite them to submit a full article. However, this does not imply that these papers will be automatically published. Rather, they will go through a peer-review process that will determine whether papers are publishable with minor or major changes, or they do not fulfil the criteria for publication.? Please send abstracts of 150 to 250 words, and 5-8 keywords by October 31, 2026, to info. diffractions@gmail.com with the subject "Diffractions 13", followed by your last name.? items.fullDescription: THE SIXTIES Call for proposals: Papers, Sessions, Panels Popular Culture Association Annual Conference March 24-27, 2027 in Boston, MA The Sixties area of the Popular Culture Association welcomes submissions for papers and presentations on any aspect of popular culture from the era. Topics of interest might include, but are not limited to: Film, television, radio, and other media (underground press, posters, etc.) Analysis of influential books/authors, art/artists, films/filmmakers, etc. New developments in religion and spirituality Psychedelia and its many manifestations The sexual revolution Music and fashion, as cultural expression and/or consumer culture New social arrangements, e.g., communes, back to the land movement 1968 or other significant dates, places, or events, e.g., Freedom Summer, Days of Rage, etc. Countercultural movements, e.g., hippies, Diggers, SDS, Black Panther Party, White Panther Party, etc.Politics and protests of the era, e.g., Civil Rights, Vietnam War, Free Speech Movement, etc. Race and gender issues, e.g., Black Power, women's rights, etc. Media representations of/reactions to any of the above Rock music, the counterculture, or other developments in international/global contexts (i.e. outside the US and UK) The significance of the decade in contemporary society and culture, including ongoing debates and revised perspectives NOTE : This year PCA is trying out a wider shared theme for the conference, on the general subject of "Revolutions and Revisions in Popular Culture" - which obviously connects with many Sixties topics. As part of that theme, presenters are invited to consider how their work might engage with questions of transformation, reinterpretation, innovation, resistance, adaptation, technological change, or changing cultural practices. Theme-related proposals are welcome but not required, and all submissions relevant to the area will receive full consideration. ALSO : This year we are also featuring a joint panel between the Sixties area and the Radio, Podcast, and Sound Media area. Possible paper topics are wide open, and could include things like: the FM radio revolution in the U.S. (freeform/progressive formats, changes in FCC policies, etc.); significant radio stations, such as WDIA in Memphis, KSAN in San Francisco, etc.; "pirate radio" in the U.K. (Radio Caroline, etc.) and official responses (the creation of BBC1, etc.); the expansion of stereophonic audio in relation to popular music, psychedelic rock, etc.; the influence of/by particular record labels on pop culture and the counterculture (especially independents such as Motown, Vanguard, ESP, etc.); more recent podcasts or other audio media about the 1960s; any of the above in non-U.S./U.K. contexts; and any other related subjects. If you would like your paper submission to be considered for the shared panel(s), please note that on your abstract or via email to the area chair. DEADLINE FOR SUBMISSIONS: October 31, 2026. For individual papers, please submit a title and 300-word abstract. Be sure to proofread your name, title, and abstract closely as this text will become part of the program should your proposal be accepted. All proposals should be submitted online via the PCA/ACA website: http://pcaaca.org More information about the submission process can be found here: https://pcaaca.org/page/submissionguidelines Inquiries about possible papers or proposals for round table sessions or full panels (including those involving the conference theme mentioned above) are also welcomed and encouraged. For themed paper sessions, each presenter must enter her/his own presentation and then contact the area chair to assemble them into a panel. All presenters must be current members of the PCA in order to submit, and must register for the conference in order to present. More detailed information about various conference matters can be found at: https://pcaaca.org/page/2027conf and elsewhere on the PCA website (check the site menus for specific topics). Please feel free to get in touch if you have any questions about topics, process, or the conference in general. Kevin M. items.fullDescription: Literary irony is a phenomenon that seems expressly invented for the approach Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate (www.connotations.de) wishes to promote, namely combining the close reading of literary texts with wider theoretical perspectives. Clearly, irony is a textual feature, and it equally clearly reaches beyond individual texts in that it evokes and reflects basic constituents of human communication: in particular, the relationship between what is said and what is meant and the relationship between what is said and what is known. Irony comes into play when these relationships are marked by significant discrepancies. The discrepancy between what is said and what is meant is essential for verbal irony and the discrepancy between what is said and what is known is fundamental to dramatic (or narrative) irony. If and how these two kinds of irony belong together, however, is a moot point and one of the questions to be addressed by our symposium. Thus the unequal distribution of knowledge (between characters and/or between characters and the reader) which marks narrative and dramatic irony may be related to the divergence which characterizes verbal irony. When Viola in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, disguised as a boy, says to Orsino: "I am all the daughters of my father's house," Orsino, who believes Viola to be a young man, must regard this statement as verbal irony on Viola's part. What is said ("daughters") is very different from what appears to be meant ("sons"). To us, the audience, however, this is a case of dramatic irony since we know that Viola is a woman and we observe Orsino's ignorance. What makes this case particularly intriguing is that here dramatic irony is not based on a discrepancy between what is said and what we know since Viola literally speaks the truth. The discrepancy arises between what we know and what is supposed to be spoken ironically. The example shows that asking about the relationship between verbal and dramatic/narrative irony entails numerous other questions that the Connotations symposium is going to address. In particular, we will ask about effects of irony, both with regard to characters and the audience. What is the added value of an ironic remark? What does it tell us about the speaker? In what way does an ironic utterance signal that there is a common ground between the communication partners? Are the inclusion and exclusion of others, i.e. those who get the ironical meaning and those who don't, similar to cases of discrepant awareness? How do we know that an utterance is meant ironically and how are we to deal with ambiguity in this respect? Can non-verbal irony markers be encoded in literary texts? Are theories of verbal irony based on notions of echo and pretence relatable to drama and fiction? We invite papers focussing on these and related questions, based on literature in English from the Middle Ages to the present. Please send an abstract (300 words max.) to the editors of Connotations at symposium2027@connotations.de by 31 October 2026

items.fullDescription: Mythology in Contemporary Culture at the Annual Conference of the Popular Culture Association Boston Marriott Copley Place March 24-27, 2027 The Mythology in Contemporary Culture area is dedicated to exploring mythological stories, figures and themes from all cultures and historical periods in all areas of popular culture. The frequent appearance of mythological motifs in popular culture speaks to the notion that mythologies, far from being relics of the past, continue to have significance. Contemporary revisionings and reinterpretations of mythological elements reflect the attitudes of current culture. Movies, television, gaming, comics, graphic novels, traditional literature, visual arts, performing arts, politics, blogs-the list goes on--hold both explicit and implicit renderings of archetypes such as Athena, Thor, Kali, and Maui, and of mythological narratives such as those found in bodies of sacred literature, classical Greek tragedies, medieval Grail legends, and culture hero narratives to name only a few examples. Proposals that pertain to the general theme of Mythology in Contemporary Culture are welcome. Potential presenters seeking inspiration for a paper topic might reflect on mythological aspects trending in media and entertainment, political currents around the world, the many "-isms" that underlie discrimination of all kinds, or the mythological aspects of a specific place (such as Boston). We will consider proposals for individual papers and/or panels organized around a theme. Sessions are 90 minutes, typically with four presenters per session. Presentations should not exceed 15 minutes. All submissions must be made through the conference submission site https://pcaaca.org/page/submissionguidelines Potential presenters must be current, paid, members of the PCA to submit proposals for the conference.For individual papers, please submit a title and 100-250 word abstract. For themed paper sessions, each presenter should enter their own proposal; for a panel proposal, each presenter should submit individually and the panel chair should contact Lol Fow with the title and a brief description of the panel and the names of the presenters. Questions about the Mythology in Contemporary Culture area may be directed to the Area Chairs: Lol Fow, efow@bmcc.cuny.edu Kate Rittenhouse, earth2k8@mac.com Important Dates to Remember: • Database opens for Submissions - Aug. 1, 2026 • Early Bird Registration Begins - Aug. 1, 2026 • Deadline for Paper Proposals - Oct. 31, 2026 • Travel Grant Applications Due - Nov. 15, 2026 • Early Bird Registration Ends for Presenters - Dec. 31, 2026 • Travel Grant Decisions / Notifications - Dec. 31, 2026 • Regular Registration Begins for Presenters - Jan. 1, 2027 • Preliminary Program draft available - Jan. 6, 2027 • Regular Registration Ends for Presenters - Jan. 31, 2027 • Late Registration Starts for Presenters - Feb. 1, 2027 Those Presenters Not Registered by Feb. 15 Will be Dropped from the Program CONFERENCE IN BOSTON, MA - March 24-27, 2027

items.fullDescription: Travelling Cultural Heritage Circulation and Digital Afterlives Call for Papers Cultural Heritage Lab International Conference 4th edition Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, Romania December 10-11, 2026 Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, as part of the FORTHEM Alliance, invites scholars, researchers, and practitioners to submit proposals for the 4th edition of the Cultural Heritage Lab International Conference, dedicated to exploring cultural heritage as a dynamic process of circulation across cultural, geographical, institutional, and historical boundaries. The 2026 edition focuses on Travelling Cultural Heritage (TCH): an approach that understands heritage not as a fixed repository, but as a process through which cultural forms, practices, ideas, and meanings move, encounter different contexts, and are transformed along the way. Drawing on Edward Said's concept of "travelling theory", Mieke Bal's "travelling concepts", and scholarship on cultural circulation, TCH shifts attention from mobile objects to the processes through which heritage is transmitted, adapted, appropriated, reinterpreted, and re-signified. Heritage travels through migration, exchange, conquest, education, trade, tourism, collecting, translation, transmedial transfer, and institutional networks. Migrants adapt cultural practices acquired abroad to their home contexts; travelling elites import fashions, recipes, and other cultural products; artistic styles acquire regional forms as they circulate; and networks of institutions, scholars, dealers, and historical circumstances determine how artefacts enter major collections. Such movements involve adaptation and transformation, but also appropriation, exclusion, and unequal centre-periphery relations. Circulation may allow heritage to acquire new meanings, but it may also entail loss. The large-scale purchase, digitisation, and destruction of books for AI training suggests a future in which physical heritage disappears while its digital avatars survive-an extreme form of travel across media and material states, combining virtual preservation with material destruction. More optimistically, AI, data science, interoperable infrastructures, and spatial visualisation can trace cultural circulation, compare contexts, and recover seemingly lost artefacts, including previously unreadable ancient manuscripts. We welcome contributions that engage with Travelling Cultural Heritage from disciplinary and interdisciplinary perspectives, including cultural and heritage studies, anthropology, archaeology, sociology, history, linguistics and literary studies, political science, art history, architecture, digital humanities, economics, media studies, religious studies, drama, film, the performing arts, museum studies, memory studies, and food studies . Contributors are invited to submit abstracts on, but not limited to, the following themes: Travelling Cultural Heritage: theories, concepts, and methodologies; Cultural circulation, transmission, adaptation, and re-signification; Heritage: migration, displacement, and diaspora; Museums, collections, objects, routes, networks, intermediaries, and infrastructures of cultural circulation; The movement of architectural forms, artistic practices, rituals, and cultural traditions; Colonial, postcolonial, and decolonial circulations of cultural heritage; Digital heritage, digital infrastructures, AI, platforms and computational approaches to cultural circulation; Heritage in translation: what changes when cultural forms travel between languages and the production of new heritage meanings Local content, foreign forms: adaptation and naturalisation across literatures; World Cultural Heritage: comparative approaches to heritage beyond national frameworks; Archaeological evidence for mobility, exchange, and cultural contacts; Memory and heritage: overlappings and differences; Case studies of cultural forms, practices, objects, ideas, or meanings that have travelled across contexts. Submission Guidelines Please submit an abstract of 250-300 words , along with a short biographical note ( max. 100 words ), to Ovio Olaru ( ovio.olaru@ulbsibiu.ro ) and Daniela Stanciu-P?sc?ri?a ( daniela.stanciu@ulbsibiu.ro ) by November 1, 2026. The organisers' decision regarding submissions will be communicated by November 15. For effectiveness, please include " Cultural Heritage Lab conference submission " in the subject line of your email. The conference will be held in English, German, and French, and will take place exclusively on-site. We look forward to your contributions! Kind regards, The organisers

items.fullDescription: Call for contributions: International Symposium organized by Nordic Summer University February 24-26, 2027 - Vilnius, Lithuania in collaboration with the Center for Psychotraumatology at Vilnius University,Performative Design Association, Luna16 Community Resource Center & Feminist Art Space ASABA The winter symposium of our NSU study circle is centered on trauma as an embodied and contested concept, and artistic practices as forms of knowledge production. We are particularly interested in how art engages with experiences of trauma beyond representation, and how bodies carry, transmit, remember, resist, and transform individual and collective histories. Theme: The Embodiment of Trauma in Artistic Practices Contemporary art has become an important site for exploring the embodiment of memory, violence, displacement, ecological loss, and collective histories. Across practices, artists increasingly investigate experiences that exceed language and resist fixed interpretation. Rather than merely representing trauma, these practices generate new ways of sensing, remembering, witnessing, resisting, and imagining together. The symposium approaches trauma as a contested concept. While informed by contemporary research in psychology, and neuroscience, it recognizes that no single discipline can fully account for how trauma is lived, embodied, remembered, or transmitted. Clinical and diagnostic frameworks have significantly contributed to understanding traumatic experiences, yet they also exist within broader institutional, political, and economic systems that shape whose suffering becomes visible, whose experiences are legitimized, and which forms of care are recognized. At a moment when concepts such as healing, resilience, and post-traumatic growth are increasingly mobilized within cultures of productivity, self-optimization, and return to normative functioning, the symposium asks what artistic practice can offer beyond narratives of repair. Questions that explore this inquiry include: ? How does trauma become embodied, and what can artistic practices reveal about this relationship? ? How are trauma, memory, and embodiment shaped by colonization, occupation, war, displacement, ecological crisis, extraction, systemic oppression, interpersonal violence, and intergenerational histories? ? How can artistic practices create spaces for mourning, care, resistance, coexistence, and collective imagination beyond dominant narratives of healing and self-optimization? ? What forms of knowledge emerge through movement, performance, ritual, material practices, sound, image, and other embodied forms? ? How can art challenge dominant narratives of pathology and create alternative ways of living with difficult histories? - Call for contributions We invite artists, researchers, filmmakers, performers, scholars, activists, body practitioners, communities of care, psychologists, and people with lived experience to enrich our dialogue. A diversity of formats is welcome and we highly encourage practice-based forms to present and share research. items.fullDescription: Consuming US Popular Culture: Media Aesthetics, Ethics and Literacy Virtual Conference | 27-28 November 2026 The consumption of popular culture and media, particularly through platforms and social networks, has become one of the most common leisure time activities worldwide, and US productions are one of the most circulated. Television series, films, videogames, TikTokers, podcasters, memes and other forms of digital culture reach global audiences and shape political identities and cultural imaginaries. Far from being mere entertainment, these texts have consequently become intertwined and virtually inseparable from the daily practices through which individuals get their news input and even their education. The purpose of this year's virtual conference is to open a space for the analysis of the ethical principles (or lack thereof) that seem to guide the construction, circulation and reception of public discourses within the popular culture ecosystem, including both more traditional mediums such as television and comics, but also the products that emerge from generative AI. Popular media content exists as a key source of information in public discourse and influences how we interpret contemporary political issues, how we teach and learn, and even how we exist and behave in society. Although media effects have long been proven to be negotiated rather than direct, the understanding of desirable aesthetics, mindless entertainment and the rhetoric used in political discussions have been hugely impacted by AI generated content. With this cultural media environment in mind, this virtual conference invites explorations of US popular culture through the perspective of media ethics, media literacy and aesthetics. We aim at establishing a space of discussion on the political, educational, ethical and social implications of contemporary media consumption through the analysis of US popular culture. The conference welcomes contributions that tackle the ethical dimensions and societal impact of US popular culture across a wide range of media forms and how they operate within the fragmented and algorithmically curated media ecosystem that we inhabit. We welcome analysis of both mainstream and independent productions, historical and contemporary texts, as well as emerging digital practices. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: × Media ethics and the social responsibilities of producers, platforms and audiences × Media literacy as a framework for analyzing contemporary popular culture × Popular culture as a case study for developing media literacy, ethical reasoning and critical thinking in education × The teaching potential behind popular media texts × Media effects and audience reception of US popular culture × Social media trends, influencers and memes × AI aesthetics in popular media × Polarization, misinformation, conspiracy narratives, and the circulation of disinformation through popular media × (Un)ethical representation of minorities × Political communication, civic engagement, and democratic participation through entertainment media × Representation of political and social problems in US popular culture Deadline for proposals: 1 November 2026 We accept abstract proposals for individual presentations (≈ 250 words), as well as full panels (3 presenters, ≈ 250-word description of the panel plus brief abstracts of all papers). Please, submit your abstract proposal via email at popmec.media@gmail.com as a single attachment (.doc, .docx, .odt) including name, affiliation (if any), and contact email.

items.fullDescription: The Whorfian invites pitches from writers, artists, translators, scholars, and close observers of everyday life. We look for clear, attentive pieces that show how language shapes what people notice, understand, make, or miss-across culture, translation, psychology, philosophy, anthropology, art, music, literature, and lived experience. We do not accept full manuscripts, press releases, or pitches already under consideration elsewhere. We especially invite concise pitches for features, which are our usual commissioned format, as well as shorter Traces, essays, and edited conversations. A good pitch is 150-250 words: the idea, why it fits The Whorfian, the format, one or two sources or examples, and a short bio. Authors retain copyright. The Whorfian's editors welcome your pitches and inquiries. Please wait at least one week before asking about a pitch you have already sent. Our editorial meetings review pitches that meet the criteria above, and we respond to everyone who follows them. Unsolicited manuscripts may not be considered; please contact us first to discuss your subject and framing. Traces - 700-750 wordsA precise, compact reading of a small cluster of elements in context-a set of expressions, a palette, symbols, or a few lines-and what they reveal about the wider scene. Whorfian essays - 1,200-1,800 wordsOur principal format: one strong argument, supported by research, examples, and clear prose. items.fullDescription: Childhood is far more than a stage of life - it is a dynamic social, cultural, historical and political construct that shapes individuals, communities and societies. The experiences, representations and rights of children influence not only personal development but also the future of education, healthcare, policy, culture and social justice. As contemporary societies grapple with rapid technological change, migration, inequality and evolving family structures, the study of childhood has become more relevant than ever. Over the past decades, Childhood Studies has emerged as a vibrant interdisciplinary field, challenging traditional assumptions about children and recognising them as active social actors with their own voices, agency and rights. Today, researchers and practitioners from across the humanities, social sciences, education, health, law and the arts are exploring childhood from diverse theoretical and methodological perspectives. This conference provides an international platform for scholars, researchers, practitioners, policymakers, educators, artists and professionals to discuss contemporary debates, emerging challenges and innovative research on children and childhood. We particularly welcome interdisciplinary approaches that bridge disciplines and offer fresh perspectives on children's lives in local and global contexts.
