items.title: CFP: Chapters for The Bloomsbury Handbook of Transecology
items.excerpt: A decade after Nicole Seymour's chapter "Trans Ecology and the Transgender Road Narrative" in The Oxford Handbook of Ecocriticism , following Susan Stryker's foreword to the 2020 book Transecology: Transgender Perspectives on Environment and Nature , and after TSQ: Transgender Studies Quarterly 's November 2024 issue on trans* ecologies , which built on t...
items.fullDescription: A decade after Nicole Seymour's chapter "Trans Ecology and the Transgender Road Narrative" in The Oxford Handbook of Ecocriticism , following Susan Stryker's foreword to the 2020 book Transecology: Transgender Perspectives on Environment and Nature , and after TSQ: Transgender Studies Quarterly 's November 2024 issue on trans* ecologies , which built on the Queer and Trans* Ecologies (QTE) Interdisciplinary Initiative symposium that drew more than six hundred participants, transecology as a field needs a comprehensive reference handbook. The Bloomsbury Handbook of Transecology will be the first such volume: covering 38 topics, organized across four sections moving outward in scale from the molecular body to the deep-time planet. All 38 topics with descriptions are listed at the end of this CFP. Trans embodiment reorganizes our sense of time and scale - through hormonal transition time, community time, and geological time - and this clustering is reflected in the Handbook itself. To preview the Handbook's overarching structure, a short Foundations section comes first, gathering topics that examine transecology's own genealogy and disciplinary boundaries. Chapters in this section stand outside any single scale - they are about the field's history and self-definition, not about a body, a community, or a planet. The three-part structure of the rest of the Handbook then begins. Part I opens at the molecular and individual scale: chemistry, sensation, the single body. Part III closes at the planetary and deep-time scale: the atmosphere, the ocean, the epoch. Part II is the connective tissue between them: community, region, law, and culture, the scale at which intimate experience becomes shared knowledge and shared knowledge becomes political. By spanning scales ranging from the body to the planet, with the mediating communal scale between these extremes, the Handbook emphasizes that transecology's center of gravity is not the isolated body or the abstract planet, but the connecting community. The senior editor of The Bloomsbury Handbook of Transecology , Douglas Vakoch, has edited over two dozen books, including Transecology: Transgender Perspectives on Environment and Nature (2020), Transgender India: Understanding Third Gender Identities and Experiences (2022), and The Routledge Handbook of Trans Literature (with Sabine Sharp, 2024). Vakoch also serves as the general editor of four book series in environmental studies and transgender studies for Bloomsbury Academic: Ecocritical Theory and Practice, Environment and Society, Critical Plant Studies, and the recently launched Trans Studies. SUBMITTING YOUR PROPOSAL Interested authors should submit a 300-word abstract, a 200-word biography, 5 key scholarly references, and a sample of a previously published chapter or article to https://bit.ly/Handbook_of_Transecology no later than November 15, 2026. Proposals submitted by email will not be accepted. Abstracts, biographies, and scholarly references should be combined into a single Word document, and previously published chapters or articles should be submitted as PDFs. Both Word files and PDFs should contain the author's name in the file names. Please include your email address in your Word document so we can contact you with our decision about your proposal. Your abstract should clearly state which of the Handbook's 38 topics is most relevant to your chapter, listing both topic number and name (see full list below). All chapters must have specifically transgender and ecological dimensions, and not merely a more broadly queer focus. In addition to the Handbook, we will also be creating standalone books on topics for which we receive an especially strong response of outstanding proposals. Your proposal will automatically be considered for both the Handbook and standalone volumes. You are welcome to submit more than one abstract. If you decide to submit multiple abstracts for different chapters, please add a note at the top of each abstract to indicate whether you wish to be considered for writing only a single chapter, or whether you wish to be considered for writing more than one chapter. The most competitive proposals will detail the author's argument. It is not enough to describe what you plan to do in your chapter. You should summarize what you will conclude. Authors will be notified whether their proposals are accepted by December 15, 2026. Partial first drafts are due by March 1, 2027; solid first drafts of full chapters are due by May 1, 2027; and final versions that cross-reference other chapters extensively are due July 15, 2027. All authors must have completed a PhD. In your 200-word biography, please note the year and university where you earned your doctorate. Only previously unpublished works will be considered. AI POLICY Contributors must adhere to the AI usage guidelines outlined in Bloomsbury's AI Policy for Authors and Illustrators ( https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/connect/contact-us/ai-policy-for-authors-and-illustrators/ ). For the purposes of this volume, "AI systems" include publicly accessible generative platforms (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, and similar tools) as well as AI-enabled grammar and editing systems. In accordance with these guidelines: • Publicly accessible AI systems (free or paid) may not be used to generate, draft, rewrite, or substantially edit submitted chapters. • Institutionally licensed or privately managed AI systems may be used solely for limited brainstorming or organizational assistance, not for composing substantive scholarly content. • Authors remain fully responsible for the originality, intellectual integrity, and scholarly accuracy of their submissions. All accepted contributors will be required to formally attest to compliance with these policies. 38 TOPICS IN TRANSECOLOGY FIELD GENEALOGY AND HISTORIOGRAPHY 1. What Is Transecology? Field Formation and Contested Boundaries Transecology's emergence as a named field - the conditions under which environmental humanities and transgender studies converged - is itself a contested intellectual history requiring critical examination. Contributors might explore competing accounts of the term's coinage and early uses; whether transecology names a method, an object of study, a political commitment, or all three; or how founding narratives shape which questions become canonical and which scholarly work gets excluded. Relevant traditions include transgender studies historiography and field-formation studies in history of science. This topic establishes the conceptual ground on which all subsequent topics depend. 2. Before Transecology: The Queer Ecology Canon and Its Afterlives Transecology builds on queer ecology while also contesting that inheritance - attending to what trans embodiment specifically adds, alters, or requires abandoning. Contributors could investigate which canonical queer ecological concepts have been carried into transecology without sufficient revision once trans embodiment is centered. They might equally well explore what is gained and lost when transecology narrates queer ecology as an enabling precursor rather than a contested interlocutor. Relevant traditions include queer theory's engagement with nature-writing and urban political ecology. This topic distinguishes transecology's genuine departures from a field it inherits. 3. Contested Inheritances: Ecofeminism, Trans Critique, and the Politics of Nature and Gender Ecofeminism and transgender theory share one of the most contested relationships in feminist thought: the gender essentialism of some forms of ecofeminism - connecting women's reproductive bodies to the Earth - provided conceptual and rhetorical resources for trans-exclusionary feminism, while trans theory's denaturalization of the sexed body challenged ecofeminism's foundational assumptions about nature, womanhood, and ecology. Contributors could interrogate the intellectual history of this antagonism and what it reveals about the limits of biological essentialism in environmental thought. Or they might explain what a trans-informed critique requires ecofeminism to revise to serve as a resource for transecology. Relevant traditions include feminist intellectual history, trans studies, and ecofeminism. PART I: INTIMATE AND EMBODIED SCALES MOLECULAR, BIOCHEMICAL, AND REPRODUCTIVE ECOLOGIES 4. Permeable Bodies: Toxicity, Contagion, and the Politics of Exposure The body is ecologically open rather than bounded - exposed to chemical compounds, viral agents, and hormonal flows that cross its supposed borders - and this permeability is differently structured by race, gender, class, and trans status. Contributors might analyze how sex-panic discourse frames both hormone disruption and viral disease in ways that stigmatize non-normative bodies. As another option, they could show how a trans-informed environmental justice framework adds to existing toxics and viral-exposure literatures. Relevant traditions include feminist science studies, environmental justice sociology, and queer HIV/AIDS historiography. This topic integrates chemical and viral exposure literatures that have historically developed in separate scholarly silos. 5. Fungal and Microbial Transecologies Mycology's disciplinary history has been shaped by anxieties about classification, mating-type multiplicity, and unnatural reproduction that parallel the anxieties organizing binary sex biology - making fungal science a queerer discipline than its institutional self-presentation admits. Contributors will examine how fungal multiplicity offers transecological theory resources distinct from plant taxonomy or animal companionship, as well as investigating what fungal transformation contributes to molecular-scale transecological thought. Relevant traditions include mycology, philosophy of science, and queer science studies. This topic opens transecology to its smallest living scales and most fundamental challenge to biological individuality. 6. Trans Reproductive and Biotechnological Ecologies Reproductive biotechnology embeds trans bodies in industrial-scale biological production - cryopreservation, IVF, and genetic screening - with ecological consequences that transecological theory has not yet systematically examined. Contributors might study how cryopreservation connects individual trans reproductive decisions to planetary cryospheric ecology, or they could ask what milieu-embedded trans reproductive ethics requires once reproductive choice is understood as constituted by chemical, ecological, and social environments. Relevant traditions include feminist science studies, reproductive ethics, and political ecology. This topic connects the most intimate scales of trans reproductive life to planetary biological systems. 7. Transecologies of Food, Agriculture, and Nutrition Food systems are profoundly gendered, racialized, and ecological, yet their specifically trans dimensions - hormonal agricultural chemistry, gendered food labor, and trans food justice - remain theoretically underdeveloped. Contributors will examine how cisheteronormative household structures organize food distribution systems in ways that marginalize trans family formations, or they might ask how agricultural hormones and endocrine-disrupting pesticides create hormonal pathways connecting trans bodies to food ecologies. Relevant traditions include environmental history, feminist geography, and trans studies. This topic also invites attention to regionally and nationally specific agricultural and culinary traditions, recognizing that food's gendered and ecological politics take distinct shape in different national contexts. This topic opens an understudied intersection where trans studies and food systems ecology must be developed together rather than as adjacent literatures. 8. Trans Vegetal Ecologies Plants challenge the foundational assumptions - about the boundaries of individual organisms, binary sexual reproduction, and self-contained subjectivity - that binary gender systems and conventional ecology share, making vegetal life a theoretically generative but underexplored site for transecology. Contributors will explore what plant philosophy's reconception of distributed subjectivity contributes to transecological theory, and they will examine how the history of plant-derived hormone chemistry connects botanical ecology to trans pharmaceutical supply chains. Relevant traditions include critical plant studies, feminist botany, and plant philosophy. This topic extends transecological analysis to forms of life routinely excluded from animal-centered frameworks. INDIVIDUAL EMBODIMENT, HEALTH, AND SENSATION 9. Tranimacies: Trans Lives, Animal Bodies, Nonhuman Genders The coupling of transness and animality that scholars have termed tranimacies generates transecological analysis across three registers: humanities-based theories about the trans-animal interface, empirical animal-companionship research, and the political stakes of analogizing trans life to animal life. Contributors might explore how trans-animal companionship functions empirically in clinical, familial, and everyday life. Alternatively, they might explain how evolutionary biologists narrate sexual diversity in nonhuman species. Relevant traditions include animal studies, multispecies ethnography, and feminist science studies. 10. Trans-Crip Ecologies: Disability, Debility, and Environmental Belonging Disability and transecological thought share an undertheorized structural affinity: both critique the assumption of an original normal bodily state, and both analyze what happens when environments fail the bodies they are supposed to sustain. Contributors could explore the curative imaginary - the logic of returning to presumed normative states - as it operates in both trans medicalization and ecological restoration. They might also consider how conservation biology's normative investments parallel the normativity that trans and disability politics together challenge. Relevant traditions include crip theory, disability justice, and environmental humanities. This topic forges transecology's most urgently needed alliance with disability studies. 11. Performativity, Trans Embodiment, and Ecological Aesthetics Performativity theory - extended from feminist philosophy - offers transecology a framework for understanding ecological processes as enacted through material-discursive practices rather than given as natural facts. Contributors might consider what it means to think of ecological processes themselves as performative, or they could choose to investigate how trans embodiment enacts gender through and alongside ecological environments in ways that transform the environments themselves. Relevant traditions include feminist performativity theory, trans cinema and literary studies, and ecomedia analysis. This topic opens transecological method to a wider range of cultural and natural objects than previous frameworks have addressed. 12. Ecological Environments and Trans Mental Health Ecological environments shape trans mental health, well-being, and healing in ways that established clinical frameworks are poorly equipped to address - making the intersection of ecotherapy, disability studies, and transecological theory an urgent but undertheorized domain. Contributors might explore how ecological grief resonates with and diverges from the forms of loss trans people navigate in transition. Alternatively, they could ask how companion animal relationships buffer the compounded stresses of cisgenderism and environmental vulnerability. Relevant traditions include ecopsychology, trans studies, and feminist disability studies. This topic opens psychological and ecological dimensions the field has insufficiently addressed. 13. The Pleasures of Re-Embodied Environmental Attunement Transition restructures sensory experience: affirmed bodies encounter temperature, season, water, and landscape differently, grounded in re-embodied attunement that extends beyond social affirmation to the more-than-human world itself. Contributors could investigate how trans writers, artists, and scholars describe the specifically ecological dimensions of the sensory recalibration of transition and the pleasure of inhabiting outdoor and natural environments in an affirmed body, as well as how these experiences differ across trans communities in the Global South, Indigenous contexts, and non-Anglophone traditions. Relevant traditions include trans phenomenology, ecocriticism, trans memoir and auto-ethnography, and environmental psychology. PART II: COMMUNAL AND REGIONAL SCALES REGIONAL, DECOLONIAL, AND COMMUNITY-SPECIFIC ECOLOGIES 14. Black Transecologies: Fugitivity, Racial Capitalism, and the Nonhuman Black trans and queer thought theorizes ecology through the linked frameworks of fugitivity, racial capitalism, and antiblackness's historical construction of the human - a construction that simultaneously defined Blackness as subhuman and nature as property to be extracted. Contributors might explore how cisgendering is itself an ecologically charged racialized construct, or they could analyze how Black feminist ecological practice constitutes knowledge that the broader field has not yet integrated. Relevant traditions include Black feminist theory, Afropessimism and its critics, and Black queer performance studies. This topic also extends to the racialized structure of mass violence, since the same logics that construct Blackness as subhuman have historically organized genocide and other forms of collective racial violence. This topic insists that Blackness and transness are co-constitutive categories within ecological thought. 15. Non-Anglophone and Global South Transecologies Transecological thinking has developed independently across multiple non-Anglophone traditions - including such varied examples as Colombian biodiversity science, Brazilian ecotransfeminismo, French activist ecology, South African queer ecological theory, South and Southeast Asian ecofeminist traditions, and Pacific Indigenous gender-ecological knowledge - generating frameworks that cannot be reduced to regional applications of Anglophone theory. This topic welcomes scholarship from any non-Anglophone tradition, including but not limited to the Global South, since non-Anglophone transecological thought has also developed within European, East Asian, and other linguistic contexts not typically classified as Global South. Contributors could investigate the breadth of non-Anglophone transecological scholarship on its own terms, focusing for example on African queer ecological frameworks, Asian engagements with transecological thought, M?ori and Pacific Islander gender-environment relations, and Brazilian, Chilean, and Caribbean decolonial ecotransfeminisms. They might also ask what is concretely lost in conceptual precision, political commitment, and genealogical complexity when transecological frameworks are translated between languages or dominated by Anglophone institutional production. This topic requires contributors to engage non-Anglophone scholarship directly rather than through secondary summary, and challenges the handbook to model the global reach of transecological thought it documents. 16. Decolonial Ecofeminism and Trans Traditions: Gender Variance, Land, and Resistance in the Global South Non-Western ecofeminism - Vandana Shiva's chipko ecology, Wangari Maathai's Green Belt Movement, Latin American pachamama traditions - and non-Western trans traditions - hijra, two-spirit, travesti, muxe - both emerged from resistance to colonial impositions of Western binary gender and extractivist land relations. Contributors could explore how decolonial ecofeminism and Indigenous trans traditions share genealogies of resistance to colonial land dispossession and binary gender enforcement. Alternatively, they might ask what transecological knowledge these convergences generate that Anglophone ecofeminism and trans studies cannot produce. Relevant traditions include decolonial ecofeminism, Indigenous studies, and Global South trans theory. 17. TransCaribbean and Latin American Ecologies Transecological thought emerging from the Caribbean and Latin America - where plantation history, hurricane ecologies, and disaster capitalism structure the relationship between gender variance and environment - requires frameworks not derivable from Anglophone settler contexts. Contributors might explore queer Caribbean speculative fiction's ecological imagination, investigate how decolonial ecofeminisms in the Southern Cone theorize trans environmental belonging differently, or consider how urban intimacy, migration, and colonial violence collectively inform transecological belonging. Relevant traditions include decolonial theory, extractive-zone critique, and Caribbean literary and cultural studies. This topic insists on language and region as organizing categories in their own right. 18. Two-Spirit and Indigenous Ecological Knowledge Beyond the Settler Frame Two-Spirit and Indigenous ecological knowledge cannot be adequately engaged as antecedent or parallel to Western trans categories - it requires engagement through its own theoretical genealogies, which refuse the nature/culture and body/environment separations that Western transecology typically operates within. Contributors might explore reciprocity-based plant and land knowledge as an independent epistemological system, or they could investigate how Two-Spirit memory critiques settler queer politics as itself a colonial formation. Relevant traditions include Indigenous studies, settler colonial studies, and Two-Spirit scholarship. This topic positions Indigenous ecological knowledge as a foundationally generative theoretical source. 19. Transecologies of Place: Geography, Home, and Belonging Where trans people live, move, and flourish is fundamentally an ecological and geographic question - different environments produce genuinely different transecological possibilities, constraints, and communities. Contributors might consider how geo-affective theory reconceptualizes the spatial analysis of trans place-making, or they could ask how rural, urban, suburban, and wilderness transecologies structurally differ in what they generate and foreclose for trans life. Relevant traditions include queer geography, feminist urban studies, and environmental justice. This topic also extends to specific regional and state-level place-identity, since attachment to a particular region or state can shape transecological belonging as concretely as the rural/urban/wilderness distinctions above. This topic insists that transecological belonging is always spatially produced, politically contested, and materially consequential. CULTURAL, LITERARY, AND SCREEN PRODUCTION 20. Trans Ecopoetics and Environmental Literature Literary and poetic practice has been among transecology's earliest and most productive knowledge-producing sites, generating ecological understanding that scholarly argument alone cannot achieve. Contributors could explore trans ecopoetics as a distinct aesthetic mode with specific formal properties - non-linear temporality, dissolved subject-object boundaries, and ecological personhood. They could equally well ask whether transecological literature constitutes a recognizable genre with both formal and thematic coherence. Relevant traditions include ecocriticism, trans literary studies, and comparative literature. This topic asks what literary form contributes to transecological knowledge that theoretical argument cannot produce. 21. Trans Ecocriticism, Medieval to Contemporary Trans ecocriticism spans at least a millennium of literary history - from medieval romance's gender-variant nature imagery through early modern natural philosophy to contemporary trans poetry - testing whether transecological reading holds as a method across radically different historical contexts. Contributors could investigate how premodern literary texts figure gender variance through ecomaterial metaphor, or they might decide to ask what continuities or ruptures exist between medieval and contemporary trans ecopoetic strategies. Relevant traditions include ecocriticism and medieval studies. This topic insists that transecological reading is not a contemporary invention but a method with deep literary precedent. This topic also welcomes attention to specific national literary traditions, since gender-variant nature imagery recurs across distinct national canons in ways that a purely period-based history can overlook. 22. Transecological Narrative, Genre, and Experimental Cinema and Television Narrative film and television - from art cinema to genre drama to experimental and animated forms - construct transecological imagination at temporal scales that nonfiction cannot achieve, and this topic welcomes contributions on fictional, hybrid, and experimental screen work across world cinema traditions. Contributors might explore how narrative and genre conventions figure the relationship between trans life and ecological environments, or they could analyze how fictional forms - including horror, comedy, melodrama, coming-of-age films, fantasy, musicals, and animation - enable distinct transecological imaginaries. Relevant traditions include trans film theory, narrative theory, genre studies, and ecocinema studies. All proposals for this topic should explain how insights from trans studies and ecocinema studies can be integrated to create a new field of trans ecocinema. 23. Transecological Documentary and Activist Screen Media: Global Nonfiction Forms Documentary and activist screen media make available to transecology what fiction and scholarship cannot: showing trans people in actual ecological relations with specific places and living systems. Contributors might investigate what transecological documentary provides across nonfiction genres - feature, short, web-distributed, activist media - drawing on any national or regional context. They might also consider how documentary traditions from Global South, Indigenous filmmaking communities, and non-Anglophone contexts - such as Brazilian trans documentary, African queer ecology films, South Asian gender-variant nature cinema, and Pacific Islander environmental media - construct transecological witnessing distinct from Western conventions. All proposals for this topic should explain how insights from trans studies and ecocinema studies can be integrated to create a new field of trans ecocinema. 24. Monstrosity, the Nonhuman, and Transecological Visual Culture Transecological visual and literary culture has reclaimed monstrosity as an affirmative aesthetic and theoretical category - proposing that what has historically been viewed as unnatural about trans bodies constitutes an ecological critique rather than a stigma to overcome. Contributors could explore how trans monsters challenge the natural/unnatural binary in fiction, horror film, and genre screen drama. As another option, they might trace how the history of monster imagery reveals transecological dimensions in visual culture that earlier criticism missed. Relevant traditions include Gothic studies, trans nonhumanism, and visual culture criticism. This topic suggests that the monstrous and the ecologically abject are affirmative transecological positions. 25. Celebration, Beauty, and Delight in Trans Ecocultural Production Transecological joy is produced in and by trans cultural practice - art, performance, ecosexual activism, trans nature poetry, and collective trans ritual in outdoor and ecological settings - and this topic examines what those cultural forms specifically enable when they center joy rather than suffering. Contributors might investigate what aesthetic strategies trans cultural producers use to claim ecological joy, or equally well, they could explore how trans joy as cultural production is evident such diverse forms as Tourmaline's Black trans joy cinema, Brazilian trans carnival ecology, South Asian hijra performance traditions, and Afrofuturist ecological celebration, among others. Relevant traditions include trans aesthetics, performance studies, ecocriticism, and cultural theory. This topic also extends to sport, festival, and embodied public celebration, since these communal, physically expressive occasions can enact transecological joy as fully as art or ritual can. LAW, AGENCY, AND TEMPORALITY 26. Transecological Jurisprudence and Rights of Nature Rights of Nature jurisprudence and trans rights jurisprudence both extend legal standing to subjects historically excluded from legal personhood - a structural parallel that transecological jurisprudence can examine with precision and political consequence. Contributors might consider what these parallel legal transformations reveal about each other's underlying assumptions regarding subjecthood, or alternatively, they could ask how decolonial and Indigenous legal traditions challenge both ecological rights and trans rights frameworks built from settler liberal foundations. Relevant traditions include environmental law, trans legal theory, and postcolonial legal studies. This topic also extends to citizenship status, human rights frameworks, and international and diplomatic legal regimes, since these too determine which subjects a legal order recognizes as bearers of standing. This topic argues that by studying ecological and trans legal transformations together, we can gain insights not accessible to either separately. 27. Beyond Essentialism and Constructionism: New Materialist Ecofeminism and Trans Theory New materialism has transformed both ecofeminism and trans theory: where early ecofeminism's gender essentialism and trans theory's social constructionism once seemed irreconcilable, feminist new materialism - Barad's agential realism, Haraway's multispecies kinship, Hird's queer non/human - creates shared ground where both traditions engage bodies, matter, and ecology without naturalizing or denaturalizing gender. Contributors could choose to explore what a new materialist synthesis of ecofeminism and trans theory looks like, or they might ask how these frameworks enable ecofeminist-trans dialogue across non-Western, Indigenous, and Global South contexts. Relevant traditions include new materialism, feminist science studies, ecofeminism, and trans theory. 28. Animacy Hierarchies and Transecology Animacy - the differential assignment of liveliness, agency, and subjecthood to different kinds of bodies - structures ecological thought in ways that systematically disadvantage trans, racialized, disabled, and nonhuman bodies simultaneously. Contributors might consider how animacy hierarchies organize ecological science, conservation practice, and their cultural representations, or they could investigate how transecological analysis reveals and contests animacy arrangements that determine who counts as an ecological subject. Relevant traditions include trans feminist materialism, animacy theory, and environmental humanities. This topic insists that who and what counts as alive for ecological purposes is a political and theoretical determination, not a natural fact. 29. Trans Temporality and Ecological Time Trans embodiment reorganizes temporal experience at multiple scales - hormonal transition time, social community time, and geological ecological time - making trans temporality a productive resource for environmental humanities. Contributors might explore how trans temporal experience generates ecological critique unavailable from frameworks that treat time as universal. As an alternative, they could ask how the relationship between trans time and geological or evolutionary ecological time can be theorized across literary and screen media. Relevant traditions include trans studies, queer temporality theory, and environmental humanities. This topic also extends to biography, oral history, and commemorative practice, since these are sites where trans and ecological temporalities visibly intersect in how a life or an era gets remembered. This topic proposes that trans temporal experience can serve as an analytical tool for ecological thinking at every scale. 30. Hope, Utopia, and the Future of Transecological Worlds Trans joy is irreducibly forward-facing - it is joy in what is not yet but might be, joy in imagining transecological worlds that do not yet exist - and this topic examines transecological joy as a form of hope, futurity, and refusal to accept crisis as the only frame for transecological imagination. Contributors might explore how trans speculative fiction, solarpunk, Indigenous futurism, and queer utopianism imagine transecological flourishing, or they could ask how ecological joy as futurity is imagined in such diverse forms as Brazilian ecotransfeminismo, Afrofuturist joy traditions, West African ecological utopianism, and Asian trans speculative imagination. This topic claims joy as transecology's most generative temporal stance. This topic explicitly names utopian and dystopian political and literary traditions as relevant precedents, since transecological hope draws on and revises a much longer history of utopian thought. PART III: PLANETARY AND DEEP-TIME SCALES ATMOSPHERE, OCEAN, AND DEEP EARTH 31. Trans Atmospheric Ecologies: Air, Breath, and Climate The atmosphere - increasingly destabilized by greenhouse emissions and industrial chemical pollution - has emerged as transecology's most urgently contested elemental domain, entangling trans bodies with chemical exposures, respiratory vulnerability, and the politics of breath. Contributors could investigate how atmospheric chemical exposure disproportionately exposes trans communities to elevated chemical burden, or they might ask what the COVID-19 pandemic revealed about atmospheric vulnerability along race, class, and gender lines. Relevant traditions include environmental justice, feminist science studies, and climate humanities. This topic connects the molecular scale of trans atmospheric exposure to the planetary scale of climate politics. 32. Aqueous Transecologies: Water, Rivers, Oceans, and the Blue Humanities Water - rivers, watersheds, oceans, tidal zones - has become transecology's most generative elemental domain, in part because water's formal properties of transition, permeability, and state change resonate across trans and ecological theories simultaneously. Contributors might explore how different water bodies configure different transecological possibilities and constraints. In addition, they could consider what Indigenous freshwater knowledge, Black trans feminist ocean ecology, and blue humanities each contribute to this domain. Relevant traditions include hydrological science, blue humanities, environmental law, and trans studies. This topic also welcomes attention to specific national and regional hydrological histories, since a particular river, coastline, or watershed can anchor transecological analysis as concretely as a global elemental frame. This topic argues that water's material properties make it transecology's most productive elemental medium. 33. Trans Geological Ecologies: Deep Time, Minerals, and Transition Geological deep time - operating at scales of millions of years - provides transecology with temporal resources that transition narratives calibrated to individual human lifetimes cannot supply. Contributors might explore how geological temporality reframes trans becoming as part of Earth's longer history of material transformation, or they could trace how trans pharmaceutical supply chains are concretely entangled with lithium mining and hormone-precursor agriculture. Relevant traditions include geology, trans studies, political ecology, and environmental humanities. This topic also welcomes attention to specific national and regional geological histories, since a particular mining region or mineral economy can ground transecological analysis as concretely as a planetary deep-time frame. This topic extends transecology's temporal horizon from individual human lifetimes to planetary deep time. 34. Trans Subterranean Ecologies: Underground Life and Becoming Underground ecologies - mycorrhizal networks, soil microbiomes, cave systems, and deep aquifers - constitute one of transecology's richest and least theorized domains, offering figures for trans becoming that operate below the surface-visibility epistemology that has dominated the field. Contributors might investigate how distributed fungal networking models for transecological community differ from organism-centered alternatives, or they could consider how decomposition and regeneration as primary biological processes help us understand transecological becoming in ways that developmental metaphors miss completely. Relevant traditions include mycology, feminist science studies, and trans theory. This topic asks what transecology learns from what happens below the surface. PLANETARY FUTURES AND SPECULATIVE COSMOLOGIES 35. Transecology and Science Fiction: Alien Life, Posthuman Biology, and Ecological Imagination beyond Earth Science fiction's biological imaginary - alien life forms, posthuman evolution, biotechnological embodiment, interstellar ecologies - directly contests the naturalistic assumptions about sex that trans people face in their healthcare, legal systems, and daily lives, making SF a uniquely powerful resource for transecological thinking. Contributors might explore how SF's imagined biologies produce transecological knowledge about non-binary sex, mutable embodiment, and ecological relations beyond the human. They could just as well consider how SF genre conventions from Japanese SF to Chinese ?? to Nigerian Africanfuturist fiction give trans characters and gender-variant ecologies formal possibilities unavailable in realist literature. Relevant traditions include SF studies, biology, and trans studies. 36. Transecological Climate Fiction: Speculative Responses to Planetary Environmental Change Trans people are among the most climate-vulnerable populations - unhoused at higher rates, dependent on pharmaceutical supply chains, subject to violence in evacuation centers - and climate fiction's engagement with planetary ecological change therefore always carries specific trans stakes that this topic makes central. Contributors could explore how climate fiction across eco-dystopia, solarpunk, Indigenous futurism, and speculative realism imagines trans survival, community, and flourishing under planetary collapse, or they might ask how climate speculative writing from Latin America, Europe, Africa, Asia, and Oceania centers transecological futures differently from Anglophone production. Relevant traditions include cli-fi studies, trans literary and film studies, and visual and plastic arts. This topic insists that climate futures are always specifically trans futures. 37. Transecological Thought and the Naming of the Epoch The ongoing debate over naming our geological-ecological epoch - Anthropocene, Capitalocene, Plantationocene, Chthulucene - is among the environmental humanities' most politically consequential controversies, and trans theory contributes a distinctive question: who is the anthropos? Contributors might explore what trans analysis reveals about the gendered subject of planetary harm, or they could consider how trans matter and materialities reconfigure ecological futures on a planetary scale. Relevant traditions include feminist philosophy, decolonial theory, and trans studies. This topic connects the most intimate scales of trans embodiment to the largest questions in environmental humanities. 38. What the More-Than-Human World Offers Transecology The more-than-human world is a vast archive of trans-affirmative biological abundance: fungi with thousands of mating types, fish that change sex in response to social conditions, plants that reproduce outside binary categories - and discovering this diversity generates a specific trans joy that transecology is uniquely positioned to theorize. Contributors could explore how trans people find affirmation and ecological belonging in the biological diversity of nonhuman sex and gender, or they might ask how these discoveries resonate across trans communities in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and Indigenous traditions with their own accounts of gender-variant nature.

But in the 2020s, corporate enshittification and government surveillance have restricted the reach of social networking tools. For example, Elon Musk’s purchase of Twitter meant that many users left X rather than adapt their activist practices to the restrictive corporate environment (Tenbarge & Collier 2024). items.fullDescription: CFP: 28th Southeast Conference for Languages, Literatures, and Film (Feb 27-28, 2027) in St. Petersburg, Florida (on the University of South Florida St. Petersburg Campus) Languages and Cultures in a Changing World: Identity, Responsibility, and Justice Abstracts for papers (and panels) are now being considered. Deadline for abstracts: Nov. 16, 2026 Selected papers will be published in a post-conference anthology. To view prior publication, visit the conference website. The SCFLLF welcomes papers on all aspects of literature, theoretical and applied linguistics, culture, philosophy, cultural history, film, other popular media, second language acquisition, and language pedagogy pertaining to non-English languages (ancient and modern). We would like to encourage (but not limit) submissions addressing our conference theme: Identity, Responsibility and Justice, in its broadest understanding. Selected papers will be published in a post-conference anthology. The humanities and the study of languages are facing changing institutional and social expectations. These changes encourage us to reconsider what work we do and the people and communities our work serves. To whom and to what, are artists, scholars and teachers accountable? How do languages, literatures, films, and other forms of cultural expression preserve or challenge established narratives and structures? How do they engage with different identities? How can they help us understand the present and/or imagine different futures? What responsibilities come with teaching and learning languages as well as with studying, interpreting, and representing other cultures? This conference invites scholars working in non-English languages, literatures, film and media, cultural studies, applied and theoretical linguistics, second-language acquisition, and language pedagogy to explore these and related questions from a wide range of disciplinary, theoretical, historical, and methodological perspectives. The conference theme, Identity, Responsibility, and Justice, is deliberately broad. Responsibility may involve our relationships with students and communities, with texts and their histories, with linguistic and cultural traditions, or with the institutions in which we teach and conduct research. Or responsibility can be interrogated with regard to artists and art, in a broad sense. Justice can also be approached in diverse ways. It may involve social justice, questions of representation and recognition, historical memory, inclusion and exclusion, or access and lack thereof to language learning. Justice may also concern translation and cultural mediation or the ways in which literature, film, language, and other cultural practices engage with conflict, inequality, trauma, discrimination, displacement, and/or social change. The SCFLLF keynote speaker is Adam Schwartz (Associate Professor of Language, Culture & Society, Oregon State University). Dr. Schwartz's research addresses Spanish language education and Spanish-English multilingualisms in the U.S. He takes particular interest in intersections of language, race and racism, wherein questions of identity, responsibility and justice persist. In addition to various articles and chapters, he has authored three books. These include Spanish So White: Conversations on the Inconvenient Racism of a 'Foreign' Language Education (2023). He is also the co-author of Aquí se habla: Centering the Local and Personal in Spanish Language Education (2025) as well as Language, Identity and Justice: The Anthropolitical Worlds of Ana Celia Zentella (2026). Some suggestions of topics and their artistic representations include: identity, responsibility, and justice represented in literature, art, film, and other forms of popular media, including social media influence of film and literature on the public and private sphere reassessing the purpose and value of language teaching expressions and perceptions of trauma in response to injustice justice in utopian fictional worlds addressing and expressing identity in the language classroom questions of identity in literature, film, the arts, and other popular media responsibility issues in production and reception of artistic expressions responsibilities associated with researching and representing cultures apart or in comparison to our own the broader influence of imaginary worlds created in film, literature, the visual arts, and other forms of media on real political and personal justice language and linguistic-related topics concerning identity, responsibility, and justice other topics Please submit a proposal (of no more than 250 words) for a single paper or a full panel (max. of 3 presentations) on the conference webpage. We can only accept online submissions. Please contact Margit Grieb (grieber@usf.edu) if you have any questions.

items.fullDescription: In this interdisciplinary conference, we seek to examine critical issues in the field of global Destination Management and Tourism Mobilities in pursuit of means, modes and practices to promote a greater Mobility Justice within, between, and beyond destinations (Sheller 2018; 2024). Situated within the Florentine context, this conference offers fertile ground for cross-pollination between Florence and other destinations concerned with how Destination Managers and Destination Management Organizations (DMOs) can be pivotal actors, agencies, and organizations committed to a more just, sustainable, and responsible mobile world. As the politics of mobility play out in real time through the bodies and streets, we see local, national and transnational governance struggle to keep pace with the impacts and drivers of climate change, urbanization, and migration. All the while we watch as mass tourism and overtourism thread impacts through micro, meso, and macro scales. Simultaneously, migrants, refugees, asylum seekers, undocumented, stateless, and trafficked persons experience increasing pressures and injustices through the same forces that support the most mobility privileged in global tourist flows. In this entangled web of mobility regimes and infrastructures, it is important to examine where travel and tourism have historically been a cultural force for promoting peace and dialogue, as much as examining where conflict, friction, and tensions have arisen from them. Destinations offer an opportunity to analyze and intervene at specific sites of human migrations and mobilities, and what in hopes of more just tourism mobilities in destinations across the world. Florence is no stranger to conflicts over tourism mobilities and tensions within its unique identity as a site of global patrimony. As a destination caught in the crosshairs of its rich past and an uncertain future in this age of polycrisis, conflicting representations and identities intersect, diverge, and weave a complex social fabric. Destination Management offers a targeted lens through which to interrogate the relation between global travel, tourism and mobility justice in Florence and beyond. As a UNESCO World Heritage Site, Florence represents a rich cultural tourism destination that is increasingly impacted by increasingly global flows and circulations of people, objects, artifacts, information, resources and capital. It has resulted in intersecting crises of housing displacement and homelessness, food insecurity, growing civil protest, increasing environmental resource and climatic constraints, uneven distribution of tourist fluxes between major and minor cultural sites, and loss of local goodwill in response to the immobilities created by tourism. This conference seeks to bring to light the complexities of questions of justice in a hypermobile world. How does one respect cultural heritage while local peoples and cultures suffer across so many dimensions, often deprived of their cultural rights, unable to access their own heritage sites? How do we support human and more-than-human futures, adaptable and responsive to environmental constraints, changes, and challenges? Many questions arise that require interdisciplinary perspectives. We invite papers to contribute to the emerging field of Destination Management, focusing on the intersections of issues in social, cultural, environmental, and mobility justice within the roles and responsibilities of Destination Managers and DMOs (Destination Management Organizations). We welcome a wide range of disciplinary perspectives and methods, including case study analyses, historical or contemporary mobilities, and theoretical contributions that are committed to exploring what Justice means within Destination Management theory and practice. Thematically, we ask contributors to examine how questions of justice can be integrated into interdisciplinary Destination Management scholarship that contend with the domains of travel and tourism. Submissions can include both normative and empirical research broadly relevant to informing questions of Justice and Mobilities, and can broadly range from social sciences, STEM, humanities, and arts fields, and present either contemporary or historical perspectives. We aim to explore where various areas of justice can be connected to the objectives of Destination Management research as a growing interdisciplinary field. We encourage scholars and practitioners to investigate the applicability of distributive, deliberative, procedural, restorative, and epistemic justice in the framework of their presented contributions. We are interested in case studies which either (A) center their analyses on Florence, Italy (or the region of Tuscany) in order to seek translatable and transversal solutions for other destinations, or (B) center on global destinations beyond that bring critical insight into the issues facing Florence. We are seeking to find "common ground" amongst the examined problem spaces that exist across destinations to build a growing literature concerned with promoting Mobility Justice within Destination Management. Theoretical contributions should include insight or practical application to transversal issues across Florence and other destinations. SUBMISSION GUIDELINES: We ask for 300-word abstracts, submitted with a separate cover page that includes title, name, affiliation, and a short bio of the author(s) of a maximum of 300 words, which can be submitted to dstm@gonzaga.edu by November 25th, 2026. The conference will be held from March 11th to 12th at Gonzaga in Florence, a school of Gonzaga University based in the historic center of the city of Florence. It will be open to the public, by registration. There will be no registration fee to attend the conference. As our inaugural conference, we are unable to offer travel funds at this time. Topical Areas: 1. Mobility Justice (motility, capabilities approach, migration, transport, space, accessibility, flows) a. Migration, refugees, stateless persons, human trafficking and modern day slavery b. Critical Disability Studies & mobility infrastructures for travel & tourism industries c. The Right to the City, labour, and yransportation equity d. Mobility, technological transformation, and electrification e. Climate Mobility Justice and immigration/refugee crises 2. Social Justice (intersectionality, human rights, kinopolitics distributive justice, reparation, processual justice) a. Indigenous Rights and Land Consent b. Human rights Abuses in the travel and tourism industry c. Intercultural exchange for responsible, sustainable, and peace tourism d. Reparative justice, public policy, media, and communications e. Critical Disability Studies and transport justice 3. Cultural Justice: (heritage studies, restoration and repatriation, cultural property, political ecology) a. Art, antiquities, museum studies, and decolonization b. Cultural heritage, human rights, and access to culture c. Cultural property trafficking, return and restitution, reclamation, and reparations d. Museum security, contemporary eco-vandalism and protest movements e. Conflicts in historiography of heritage and Post-conflict reconstruction 4. Environmental Justice (environmental racism, geoengineering, pollution and carbon, biodiversity and reparations, More-than-human ethics): a. National parks, seascapes, urban green space, and depavement movements b. Plastic pollution, chemical colonialism, exposomics, and water protectors c. Protected habitats, ecotourism and politics of spared or shared land d. Agriculture, food Justice, "The Commons", land sovereignty, and eco-activism e. Botanical gardens, zoos, "beasts of burden", and more-than-human mobility Conference Organizers: Denise Regina Percequillo Hossom Gonzaga University Alesia Koush Gonzaga University UNESCO Chair - University of Siena

items.fullDescription: “Culture,” notes Raymond Williams, “is one of the two or three most complicated words in the English language” (87). Its etymological root in cultivation—the tending and propagation of life—signals a resistance to being contained. Classroom pedagogy encompasses various elements into it—mythology, rituals, religion, tradition; movies, songs, literature; fashion, food, art—classifying it as ‘a whole way of life.’ Yet, culture surpasses being merely a way of life; it represents a way of understanding life and saturating existence with meaning. In the 19th Century, Matthew Arnold viewed culture as a framework supporting liberal humanist ideology, which aimed to prescribe a universal definition of excellence.

items.fullDescription: We invite proposals for papers from scholars of literature, theology, and philosophy to explore the intersection of St. Thomas Aquinas' thought and the dramatic works of William Shakespeare. The age of Shakespeare was steeped in and shaped by the intellectual contributions of Aquinas (informed by Aristotle), but little critical attention has been paid to the connections between the Angelic Doctor and the Bard. We seek to bring their works into rich and sustained dialogue with one another, so as to inspire a fresh critical engagement with both thinkers. To complement our keynote address by Hannibal Hamlin (The Ohio State University), we welcome papers that use Aquinas as an interpretive lens for Shakespearean drama; draw on Shakespeare to illustrate or complicate Aquinas' understanding of human and divine realities; address the broader historical, theological, and philosophical contexts linking the two figures (including their shared reception of Aristotle). Topics may include, but are not limited to: An analysis of a particular virtue or vice, as understood by Aquinas, found on the Shakespearean stage. The dramatization of other elements of Thomistic anthropology. Aquinas and Shakespeare's respective receptions of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics . The approach Aquinas and Shakespeare each takes toward Scripture. Other theological themes in the works of Shakespeare and Aquinas, such as divine providence and free will; temptation and sin; grace, conversion, redemption, and salvation; natural law and positive law. items.fullDescription: Living with the Wild: Wildlife, Civilization, and the Trouble of Coexistence University of Catania, 1-3 March 2027 Abstract deadline: 30 November 2026 The final conference of the WILD-CONNECT project, Wildlife Circulation and the Enactment of Civilization in Diachronic Perspective, invites contributions exploring how relations between the "wild" and the "civilized" have been shaped across historical, political, and cultural contexts. The conference approaches these categories as historically produced and mutually constitutive, and examines how their boundaries are continually renegotiated through institutions, practices, imaginaries, and material forms of life. We welcome contributions from anthropology, history, political ecology, environmental humanities, and related fields addressing wildlife circulation, control, transformation, and reintroduction, as well as the interconnected processes of dewilding and rewilding. Possible topics include domestication, conservation and ecological restoration; colonial and postcolonial wildlife governance; sovereignty, borders and wildlife circulation; everyday encounters with wildlife; scientific, legal and economic classifications of living beings; and the unintended consequences and limits of wildlife governance. The conference will feature keynote contributions by Vanessa Manceron (CNRS), Marcy Norton (University of Pennsylvania), and Erik Gómez-Baggethun (Norwegian University of Life Sciences). Accepted papers will be circulated among participants in advance, and contributions presented at the conference will be considered for inclusion in a collective volume or a special issue of an international journal in environmental humanities. Living_with_the_Wild_Call Please submit: an abstract of 300-400 words; a short biographical note of 100-150 words; institutional affiliation, if any, and contact details. items.fullDescription: Over the past three decades, fan studies have developed sophisticated accounts of participatory culture, collective intelligence, affective engagement, and transformative practices (Jenkins 2006; Booth 2015; Hills 2017). At the same time, scholarship has increasingly addressed the investigative dimensions of audience participation. Mittell’s concept of “forensic fandom” (2009), for example, highlights practices of close reading, clue collection, speculation, and collaborative interpretation in response to complex narrative worlds. Fans thus become active investigators who uncover hidden meanings, solve mysteries, and assemble fragmented information across media texts. More recently, such investigative practices have expanded beyond fictional worlds.

items.title: Globally Contested Imaginaries: Power and Tensions in the AI Era
items.excerpt: Globally Contested Imaginaries: Power and Tensions in the AI Era April 8-9th 2027 at the Annenberg School for Communication at the University of Pennsylvania Organized by the Center on Digital Culture and Society AND the Center for Advanced Research in Global Communication at the University of Pennsylvania AI does not enter the world as a stable technolog...
items.fullDescription: Globally Contested Imaginaries: Power and Tensions in the AI Era April 8-9th 2027 at the Annenberg School for Communication at the University of Pennsylvania Organized by the Center on Digital Culture and Society AND the Center for Advanced Research in Global Communication at the University of Pennsylvania AI does not enter the world as a stable technology with a single meaning. It is narrated, simultaneously and contradictorily, as inevitable progress, geopolitical threat, overhyped fad, development solution, environmental danger, creative partner, engine of extraction, force of displacement, or instrument of sovereignty. Its invocation reflects cultural specificity and global variance. Yet AI imaginaries, advanced by powerful actors with unequal yet unfixed power across the globe, aim to define what AI is and will become. However these projections do not travel unchanged or unchallenged; they are contested, appropriated, refused, and reconfigured across different geopolitical, cultural, linguistic, and material worlds. This symposium begins from the premise that AI's global significance is neither self-evident nor uniform. We approach AI as a global digital communication project that interrogates how technologies circulate and how their meanings are (re)assembled and contested as they move across different cultural and global contexts. We aim to address the slipperiness of AI: How does the moral valence of AI shift depending on the answers and tasks demanded of it across various contexts? What is gained and lost when AI is treated as a coherent entity rather than a contested terrain? Where do dominant and alternative AI imaginaries collide most visibly-and what do those collisions reveal about power, culture, human agency, labor, development, modernity and possibility in our present moment? We invite submissions that examine the worlds in which AI becomes imaginable and contestable: the differing global narratives, infrastructures, histories, and communicative practices that make it appear necessary, desirable, dangerous, or inevitable, as well as the counternarratives, movements, and alternative imaginaries that challenge such claims and propose other futures. In this symposium, we seek a range of scholarship that takes the asymmetries of power seriously and explores and challenges which visions of AI get amplified, resourced, and institutionalized-without treating those asymmetries as settled outcomes. We invite submissions from scholars working on the intricacies of AI's entanglements with one of the four panel subthemes below and are particularly open to receiving projects that reflect on the cultural specificity and global variances of these subthemes. Panels: Myths and Narratives Writing on the grand promises that encircle new technologies, Vincent Mosco contends, "Myths are not true or false, but living or dead." In line with this provocation, this panel invites papers that explore the various myths and narratives that animate AI imaginaries-past, present, and future. ? How do people imagine AI in ways that are particular to their local geopolitical context? ? How do race, ethnicity, class, and geography affect how AI narratives cohere and how far they travel? ? How might values-political, religious, or otherwise-inform how people conceptualize the purpose of AI? ? What types of hopes and fears are projected upon AI? What role do institutions play in the formation (and challenging) of AI narratives? ? What is the historical context or ideology at play with words like "AGI" or "superintelligence"? Labor Following the iPhone across its life cycle, Qiu, Gregg, and Crawford (2014) contend that the labor of making, designing, using, and managing digital technologies form one connected circuit, not separate worlds, of work. In the spirit of their theory of the "circuits of labour," this panel invites submissions that investigate the unequal, extractive, and interdependent labor practices and conditions of the AI era. ? How does AI interface with existing labor practices and hierarchies? ? How do workers themselves understand their relationship to AI: as displacement, augmentation, exploitation, or opportunity? How do they respond? ? How are certain forms of work sustaining AI's apparent autonomy (e.g., content moderation, data annotation, model training) narrated-or erased-in dominant accounts? How is their role being reasserted from below? ? What forms of infrastructural labor are marshaled for the growth of AI systems? In what ways is this relationship economically, socially, and environmentally relevant? ? How does the global division of AI labor map onto, reproduce, or unsettle older (asymmetric) economic geographies and relations? ? What happens to professional identity and expertise when AI is positioned as "superintelligence" or as a creative and intellectual "partner"? ? What light might earlier eras of automation or displacement anxiety (e.g., industrialization, computerization, offshoring) shed on our present moment? Resistance In this panel, we seek to understand resistance through Adorno's conceptualization of negative dialectics, wherein resistance functions neither by proposing a new, 'positive' alternative or by retreating to a naive notion of 'authentic' human nature. Rather, it operates precisely through contradiction as a critical force. We invite work that examines resistance to AI as a contradictory field, where forms of refusal, critique, and opposition reveal the limits of totalizing discourses, operate through the very systems they contest, and remain unsettled by the absence of a conclusive alternative. Submissions that address and expand on the following topics are welcome: ? How do practices of resistance challenge the exclusions, assumptions, and forms of domination in totalizing accounts of AI technological progress that seek to naturalize computational forms of classification, prediction, and control? ? How do forms of resistance to AI that expose the contradictions of totalizing technological discourses confront their own implication within these systems? In other words: How do forms of resistance to AI negotiate the contradiction of opposing AI systems, when the infrastructures, categories, and practices that enable critique may themselves be shaped by technological rationality? ? What does resistance to AI in various regions of the Global Majority at the present conjuncture reveal about the contradictions of global capitalism and how histories of colonialism continue to shape contemporary struggles over technology, sovereignty, and competing visions of modernity? Social Life This panel explores social life as another contested terrain of AI's reach and impact. We invite papers that address how global communities merge their nuanced adoption and relationship to AI with the habits, relationships, and expectations of everyday life. ? How does AI become ordinary through practices of scrolling, posting, sharing, and messaging? When is its presence noticed, questioned, or taken for granted? ? How do memes and everyday conversations make AI appear useful, threatening, intimate, or irrelevant across different cultural worlds? ? How do pleasure, pain, desire, and other embodied experiences exceed the categories through which platforms make people knowable? ? How do people negotiate intimacy, care, and belonging through media platforms and what happens to expectations of trust and reciprocity when an interlocutor may not be human? ? How are authenticity and recognition negotiated when expressions of self may be generated or curated by AI? Whose languages and ways of life become recognizable, and whose are obscured? All four panels welcome submissions from scholars, students, activists, and independent researchers working in communication and media studies, sociology, political economy, science and technology studies, information studies, cultural studies, area studies, and other related fields. Submissions are open to contributors at all career stages, but we encourage work from early-career scholars and those whose work may sit outside conventional academic structures. Submissions may take the form of a traditional paper, both theoretical and empirical, or adopt a more multimedia/modal approach. Submission Guidelines: Paper Submissions: We invite panelists to submit an extended abstract of no more than 800 words, outlining how their project relates to the symposium, as well as their methods, findings and theoretical contributions. Please include your name, affiliation, a short 100-word biography, and the specific panel to which you are interested in applying. Multimedia and Hybrid Submissions: Please submit an abstract of 800 words explaining how your piece relates to the symposium theme. For multimedia works, explain how text and other elements interact. Please include your name, affiliation, a short 100-word biography, and the specific panel to which you are interested in applying. Please send all submission materials to globallycontestedimaginaries@gmail.com by 5:00PM on December 3rd, 2026. The organizing committee will notify panelists of decisions by January 15th, 2027. If accepted, panelists will be expected to submit a full paper or project by early March. Finished multimedia submission should include a link to the project when relevant. After submission of the final project, panelists will present their work at the symposium on April 8th-9th at the Annenberg School for Communication at the University of Pennsylvania. Partial travel funding may be available for invited panelists who qualify pending budget availability.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS The Artificial Body: Cyborgs, Clones and Humanoids in Literature and Media Edited by ?rem Atasoy and Habib Tekin The edited volume The Artificial Body: Cyborgs, Clones and Humanoids in Literature and Media seeks to explore representations and conceptualizations of artificial, technologically modified, replicated, and human-like bodies from interdisciplinary perspectives. Rather than approaching the artificial body merely as a product of technological development, the volume considers it as a cultural and semiotic site through which changing ideas of embodiment, identity, agency, consciousness, corporeality, and human-machine relations are negotiated. Cyborgs, clones, androids, humanoid robots, synthetic beings, technologically augmented humans, and other forms of artificial or hybrid embodiment have long occupied the cultural imagination. Their representations raise fundamental questions concerning the limits of the human: Where does the human body end and the artificial begin? What happens to identity when the body can be modified, replicated, reconstructed, or manufactured? How do artificial bodies challenge established distinctions between subject and object, organism and machine, self and other? And how do literature and media participate in constructing, questioning, or transforming these boundaries? Situated at the intersections of literary studies, media studies, cultural studies, semiotics, philosophy, and posthumanist and transhumanist thought, the volume welcomes both theoretical contributions and analyses of individual or comparative works. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: · cyborgs and hybrid embodiment · clones, replication, and biological identity · humanoids, androids, and human-like artificial beings · artificial bodies and posthuman subjectivity · transhumanism and technological enhancement · human-machine boundaries · embodiment and artificial intelligence · synthetic and technologically constructed bodies · body modification and augmentation · artificial bodies and questions of identity, memory, and consciousness · the body as sign and the semiotics of artificial embodiment · gender, sexuality, and artificial bodies · artificial bodies in science fiction and cyberpunk · utopian and dystopian representations of technologically transformed bodies · virtual, digital, and simulated bodies · avatars and disembodied/re-embodied identities · artificial bodies and questions of agency and autonomy · the uncanny, the monstrous, and the artificial human · ethics and politics of creating, modifying, and replicating bodies · historical transformations in representations of artificial humans Contributions may examine literary texts, films, television series, graphic narratives, video games, digital narratives, or other relevant media and may employ approaches from literary and cultural studies, media and film studies, semiotics, multimodality, narratology, posthumanism, transhumanism, critical theory, gender studies, or related fields. The volume will be published as part of Interdisciplinary Studies on Philology by Maurer Press, an interdisciplinary series bringing philological research into dialogue with contemporary approaches from literary, linguistic, cultural, media, and related fields. Submission Guidelines Abstract length: 300-500 words Include: title, author name, affiliation, ORCID Formatting: Times New Roman, 12 pt, 1.5 line spacing Abstract submission deadline: December 4, 2026 CPC: The CPC for publication in this volume is 150 Euro per chapter. Publisher: Maurer Press, Germany Important Notes Full chapter length, style sheet, and timeline will be communicated upon abstract acceptance. All submissions should be original and not under consideration elsewhere. The editors and publisher reserve the right to make final selections based on peer review and fit with the volume. Please send abstracts and inquiries to: irem.atasoy@istanbul.edu.tr and habib.tekin@marmara.edu.tr

items.fullDescription: EUROPEAN SHAKESPEARE RESEARCH ASSOCIATION Congress, Shakespeare and Form: 'To set a form upon desired change' Bangor University, Wales, 27-30 July 2027 CALL FOR PAPERS : Seminar 9, Forms of Shakespeare's Diplomacy Convenors: Nathalie Rivère de Carles (Université Toulouse Jean Jaurès), France & Helen A. Hopkins (Birmingham City University, UK) This seminar investigates Shakespeare's diplomacy as a set of theatrical, political, and cultural forms: embassies, intelligence networks, ceremonial encounters, negotiated speech, translation, performance, heritage display, and later uses of Shakespeare as cultural capital. It will explore: · how diplomacy within Early Modern plays depends on forms: letters, reports, oaths, staged audiences, theatrical entertainments, curatorial narratives, and embodied performances of civility or threat · how drama stages the fragile procedures by which states, courts, and individuals form relations across difference · how playing companies have performed and/or participated in diplomacy from the early modern era until now (performing for ambassadors, negotiating patronage, censorship, audience reception, and transnational theatrical exchange, operating as cultural intermediaries through international festivals, touring productions, education programmes…) · formal and informal ambassadorship from early modern times until now, and the models of negotiation generated through varied uses of Shakespeare's works and cultural capital · how Shakespeare becomes an object of heritage diplomacy: curated through archives, museums, anniversaries, diplomatic/commemorative monuments, exhibitions, festivals, and touring productions that present him as a shared cultural inheritance while often reproducing hierarchies of nation, empire, race, gender, and class · how plays and institutions produce diplomatic knowledge: teaching audiences to read gestures, decode equivocation, evaluate testimony, and imagine political community beyond national borders The discussion will move from early modern diplomatic forms to Shakespeare's afterlives in official cultural diplomacy, public diplomacy, soft power, and heritage policy. Attention will also be given to deformation: failed negotiations, distorted information, imperial appropriation, and the conversion of cultural prestige (soft power) into political force (as cooperation or coercion). The wider aim is to reassess "Shakespearean diplomacy" as both an early modern practice of relation-making and a modern instrument whose global circulation may enable conversation, domination, or critique. In this way, we engage with the discourse around the decolonisation of Shakespeare. This process will therefore be treated not as the rejection of Shakespeare, but as a method for interrogating the colonial uses of the "Bard," recovering plural performance traditions, and rethinking heritage as a contested diplomatic space. By bringing together approaches from literary criticism, theatre history, performance studies, critical heritage studies, gender studies, race studies, and new diplomatic history, the seminar asks whether Shakespearean drama merely reflects diplomatic culture or actively theorises it. Abstracts (250-500 words) should be sent to both nrivere@univ-tlse2.fr and helen.hopkins3@bcu.ac.uk by 4th December 2026 Acceptance notification: 16th December 2026. Details about the Congress can be found here: https://www.bangor.ac.uk/sah/the-european-shakespeare-research-association-esra-2027
